rationale: The earlier conclusion says the reader is no longer a slave but a son and heir through God. The freedom exhortation now names Christ setting us free and forbids returning to a slavery yoke. The son/heir statement and the command to stand remain distinct.

The later statement says that in Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has strength, but faith working through love does. It supplies the positive contrast to the warning about receiving circumcision and Christ being of no benefit, without making uncircumcision itself the saving alternative.

Both relate a person to the whole law rather than an isolated point. Galatians makes receiving circumcision an obligation to do the whole law; James says stumbling at one point makes the whole-law keeper guilty of all. The conditions and stated consequences differ.

The earlier argument says that if righteousness comes through law, Christ died for nothing, while refusing to set aside grace. Here seeking justification by law is described as being severed from Christ and falling from grace. The shared incompatibility is stated through different consequences.

Both associate the Spirit with waiting in hope. Romans speaks of the Spirit firstfruits and waiting for adoption and bodily redemption, then unseen hope with endurance; Galatians names awaiting the hope of righteousness by the Spirit through faith. Their stated objects of waiting are retained.

Both deny decisive value to circumcision and uncircumcision. Galatians sets faith working through love over against those marks in Christ; Corinthians names keeping God commands. The positive formulations are related but not exchanged as identical wording.

The earlier astonishment at turning toward a different gospel names people troubling the readers and wanting to distort Christ gospel. Here Paul describes formerly running well and asks who hindered obedience to the truth. The link concerns their disturbed course without supplying a personal name for the hinderer.

The One who calls the readers is distinguished from this persuasion. The opening rebuke likewise places their turning to a different gospel against the One who called them in Christ grace. The connection identifies the opposed calling and diversion without assigning the persuasion an unprinted named author.

Both state that a little leaven leavens the whole batch of dough. Corinthians applies the proverb in its rebuke of boasting amid sexual wrongdoing; Galatians places it in the argument about contrary persuasion. The repeated saying does not make the two situations identical.

The opening names troublers distorting the gospel and pronounces a curse on preaching contrary to what was received. Here Paul combines confidence about the readers with judgment for the one troubling them, whoever he is. No particular troubler or additional penalty is identified.

Both connect proclaiming the crucified Christ with a stumbling block. Corinthians names the Jewish response alongside Gentile foolishness; Galatians argues that continuing persecution would be inexplicable if Paul still proclaimed circumcision and the cross stumbling block were removed. The particular audiences and argument differ.

Both use polemical bodily-cutting language in an argument about circumcision and confidence in the flesh. Galatians expresses the wish about those unsettling the readers; Philippians warns about mutilation and contrasts it with worship by God Spirit and boasting in Christ. The wish is not converted into an instruction to the readers.

Both warn against using freedom as a cover or opportunity for wrong and join freedom to service. Peter names freedom not covering evil and being God slaves; Galatians opposes a base for the flesh and commands serving one another through love. The persons served and exact images differ.

Galatians cites loving the neighbor as oneself, the command printed in Leviticus. Leviticus also forbids vengeance and bearing a grudge and names the Lord; Galatians places the saying in its claim about fulfilling the whole law. The latter claim is not inserted into Leviticus.

Both describe conflict among the addressed people through aggressive imagery. Galatians warns that mutual biting and devouring may consume one another; James asks about wars and fights and names desires, envy and quarreling. The different images and explanations are preserved.

Both oppose a walk according to the Spirit to the flesh. Romans names the law requirement fulfilled in those so walking and contrasts the objects of their minds; Galatians promises that walking by the Spirit will not fulfill flesh desire. The stated effects are kept distinct.

Both oppose flesh-directed life to the Spirit. Romans develops the flesh mind hostility toward God and inability to please Him, against Spirit life and peace; Galatians speaks of opposing desires and not doing what one wants. The two accounts are not made an identical psychological description.

Both explicitly describe people being led by the Spirit. Romans calls those led by God Spirit His sons; Galatians says those led by the Spirit are not under law. Their stated consequences remain distinct.

Both specifically name sexual immorality and impurity among practices to reject. Colossians commands putting earthly members to death and adds passion, evil desire and greed; Galatians calls its list works of the flesh and here also names licentiousness. The lists are not silently harmonized.

Both list strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger and selfish ambitions among destructive community conduct. Corinthians expresses fear about what Paul may find on arrival; Galatians continues the works-of-flesh list, including idolatry and sorcery. The differing items and settings remain distinct.

Both warn that people practicing specified wrongs will not inherit God kingdom and explicitly include drunkenness. The lists differ: Galatians here names envies and revelries with similar things; Corinthians includes its own longer set. No unprinted murders item is added to Galatians.

Both use fruit imagery for good qualities and explicitly name goodness. Galatians names fruit of the Spirit and its own list; Ephesians names fruit of the light with goodness, righteousness and truth. Light and Spirit are not substituted for each other.

Gentleness and self-control continue the immediately preceding fruit-of-the-Spirit list, whose love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness and faithfulness supply the earlier items behind such things. The no-law-against-them statement belongs to the continuation and is not supplied as wording of the preceding unit.

Both connect belonging to Christ with a crucifixion image concerning the former sinful life. Romans says the old human being was crucified with Him so the body of sin might be nullified and slavery to sin end; Galatians says Christ own people crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. The subjects, objects and grammatical actions differ.

Living by the Spirit is followed by the exhortation to keep in step with the Spirit. The earlier instruction to walk by the Spirit and not fulfill flesh desire supplies the same conduct contrast. It does not make the two conditional and imperative formulations identical.

Both reject self-exalting relations within the community. Philippians opposes selfish ambition and empty conceit with humility toward others; Galatians rejects conceit, provoking and envying one another. The positive instruction and specific prohibitions differ.

Both call for gentleness in dealing with someone in error. Timothy names the Lord slave patiently correcting opponents in hope of repentance; Galatians calls spiritual people to restore an overtaken person while watching their own temptation. The addressed roles, kinds of error and surrounding cautions remain distinct.

Romans tells the strong to carry the weaknesses of those without strength and seek the neighbor good, following Christ not pleasing Himself. This gives a concrete mutual-support comparison to carrying one another burdens and fulfilling Christ law. The different burden/weakness language and law formulation are not collapsed.

Both oppose an inflated assessment of oneself. Romans calls for sober thought instead of thinking above what one ought, in relation to apportioned faith; Galatians calls thinking oneself something while nothing self-deception. Their qualifications and immediate settings remain distinct.

Both direct examination toward oneself. Corinthians tells the readers to test and examine themselves concerning faith and Christ in them; Galatians tells each to test his own work rather than ground boasting in comparison with another. The objects of testing and stated consequences differ.

Each carrying his own load corresponds to each giving an account of himself to God in Romans. This relates individual responsibility without treating Galatians load as an exhaustively defined final-judgment image or cancelling its command to carry one another burdens.

Galatians directs the instructed person to share good things with the instructor. Corinthians relates sowing spiritual things to receiving material support from the recipients. The teaching-and-sharing relation is concrete without fixing a fee or reducing all good things to money alone.

Both state a relation between sowing and reaping. Corinthians uses sparse and generous sowing in its giving appeal; Galatians says God is not mocked and whatever a person sows he will reap, elaborated through flesh and Spirit. The comparison supplies no general promise of financial enrichment.

Both contrast flesh-directed conduct ending in death or corruption with Spirit-related life. Romans speaks of living according to flesh versus putting body practices to death by the Spirit; Galatians uses sowing and reaping and explicitly names eternal life. The actions and outcome terms remain distinct.

Both tell the brothers not to grow weary in doing good. Galatians adds reaping in the proper season if they do not give up; Thessalonians does not print that reaping clause. The shared instruction is retained with each original continuation.

Both describe the believing community through a household image. Ephesians replaces stranger status with fellow citizenship and God household; Galatians commands doing good to everyone with special attention to the household of faith. The comparison does not restrict doing good to believers only.

Both call attention to Paul own handwriting. Galatians names the large letters; Thessalonians identifies the own-hand greeting as a sign in each letter. Neither a medical cause for the large letters nor the extent of the Galatians autograph is supplied.

The earlier rhetorical question connects still proclaiming circumcision with whether persecution and the cross stumbling block would remain. Here Paul attributes the pressure to receive circumcision to avoiding persecution for Christ cross. The comparison connects the stated issue without naming the advocates or supplying additional motives.

relationship: law obligation and charged failure contrast
rationale: The earlier testimony obligates the man receiving circumcision to do the whole law. Here Paul says the circumcision advocates do not themselves keep law while seeking to boast in the readers flesh. The connection contrasts obligation and the stated failure without assigning that charge to every circumcised person indiscriminately.

Both direct boasting toward the Lord rather than human grounds. Corinthians places believers in Christ and cites boasting in the Lord; Galatians specifies the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ and adds the mutual world/crucifixion image. That additional world statement is not inserted into Corinthians.

Both expressly name a new creation in relation to Christ. Corinthians contrasts old things passing with the new; Galatians contrasts new creation with circumcision and uncircumcision counting for anything. The old/new and circumcision formulations remain distinct.

The cross-centered boasting and new-creation-over-circumcision statements supply the immediate printed context before keeping in step with this rule. The link locates that rule within the preceding argument without claiming an independently repeated peace blessing or resolving the identity and scope of the Israel of God.

relationship: carrying identification with Jesus in the body
rationale: Both use carrying language in relation to Jesus and the speaker bodily life. Corinthians says carrying Jesus dying in the body so His life may be manifested there; Galatians says Paul carries Jesus marks in his body. The link does not identify particular injuries as the marks or add a new account of their origin.

relationship: shared grace with your spirit closing
rationale: Both close with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ directed to the recipients spirit. Galatians also names brothers and prints Amen. The shorter Philippians original is not expanded with those words.
